To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of a high dose of contrast is associated with increased risk of renal complications across the spectrum of patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).

the use of a high dose of contrast medium is associated with increased risk of contrast induced nephropothy and nephropathy that requires dialysis, throughout the range of predicted risk and baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate.

the use of a high dose of contrast is associated with increased risk of contrast induced nephropathies (CIN) and nephropathy that requires dialysis (NRDs) across the continuum of predicted risk for CIN and creatinine clearance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the association between contrast volume and contrast induced nephropaty in patients with varying predicted risk of CIN following contemporary PCI.
the association between contrast volume administered during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and renal complications.
the association between contrast use and the occurrence of renal complications following coronary angioplasty.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a high contrast dose (defined as >3x CCC) is associated with increased risk of CIN in all patients, including those with a low baseline predicted risk and normal baseline creatinine.

the use of a high dose of contrast is associated with increased risk of CIN in a wide spectrum of patients, but that the magnitude of this association is dependent on baseline risk of CIN, and that this risk can be reduced by reducing contrast dose.
a high contrast dose (CV>3x calculated CCC) is associated with an increased risk of contrast induced nephropathies in patients at varying baseline risk of CIN.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of contrast nephropathy is increased by a higher contrast dose, but that this risk is also increased by the patient’s underlying kidney function and the risk of the procedure.
the contrast volume to calculated creatinine clearance ratio is a better predictor of contrast nephropathy than either variable alone.
the contrast dose used in contemporary PCI practice is associated with an increased risk of CIN in all patients, including those at low baseline risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of CIC is not limited to high risk patients, and that the risk is increased in patients with lower baseline predicted risk of CIN.
the contrast dose should be minimized in all patients undergoing coronary angiography and/or intervention.
the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy (and nephropathy requiring hemodialysis) is higher with higher contrast volume, and this is true across all risk strata.
